title: The Farming Revolution: The Deal That Built Civilization
subtitle: Around 12,000 years ago humans started planting seeds. It made us richer, sicker, more numerous, and more unequal — all at once. Everything after starts here.
hook: For about 200,000 years, humans were foragers: small bands walking the land, taking what nature offered. Then, around 12,000 years ago, in a few places at once, people did something new — they planted seeds and waited. It sounds mundane. It was the most consequential decision our species ever made. Farming didn't just feed people; it created **surplus**, and surplus created cities, kings, writing, taxes, and inequality. This is lesson one of the History track because almost every institution we'll study was born from this single shift.

sections.heading: From taking to producing
sections.body:
Foragers ate what they found. Farmers *produced* food — and crucially, produced **more than they immediately needed**. That extra is the hinge of history: **surplus**.

Surplus meant not everyone had to hunt for dinner. For the first time, some people could do *something else* full-time: make pots, forge tools, fight, pray, rule, record. Specialization was born. And specialization is the engine behind every complex society that followed.

sections.caption: The chain reaction: farming creates surplus, surplus frees people from food production, and that cascades into everything we call civilization.

sections.label: It happened more than once
sections.body: Farming was invented **independently** in at least seven regions — the Fertile Crescent, China, Mesoamerica, the Andes, and more — over thousands of years, with no contact between them. When many separate peoples stumble onto the same idea, it's a sign the conditions (a stable, warming climate after the last Ice Age) were ripe. History often rhymes because circumstances, not just individuals, drive it.

sections.label: The bargain had a dark side
sections.body: Early farmers were often **worse off** as individuals than foragers: they worked longer hours, ate a less varied diet, were shorter, and caught new diseases from crowding and livestock. Stored surplus could also be seized — enabling taxes, warfare, and the first real inequality. Farming won not because it made people happier, but because it made *more* people and more power. Some historians call it 'history's biggest fraud'.

sections.caption: Crash Course World History's classic opener on the Agricultural Revolution and the trade-offs it forced.

sections.heading: Why it's the root of this track
sections.body: Every institution we'll examine — money, writing, law, states, empires — traces back to the problem of managing surplus and the people it fed. Writing began largely as **accounting** for stored grain and traded goods (that's lesson two). States arose to **control and defend** surplus. Money became a way to move it around. Keep the chain in mind — surplus → specialization → complexity → institutions — and the rest of history reads as variations on this theme.

takeaways: ~12,000 years ago humans shifted from **foraging to farming** — producing food, not just finding it.
Farming's real product was **surplus**: more food than immediately needed.
Surplus freed people to **specialize**, and specialization built villages, cities, and states.
It arose **independently in several regions**, pointing to shared conditions (post-Ice-Age climate).
The bargain was harsh — worse individual health, disease, and new inequality — but it produced more people and power, so it spread.

quiz.q: What was the pivotal *economic* consequence of farming that set off everything else?
quiz.explain: Producing more food than you immediately need — surplus — is what freed some people from food-gathering and enabled specialization.

quiz.q: What does it tell us that farming was invented independently in several parts of the world?
options: One civilization taught all the others
It was pure luck each time
Broad conditions (like the post-Ice-Age climate), not single individuals, drove the change
It only happened in the Fertile Crescent
quiz.explain: Independent invention in many places suggests the underlying conditions were ripe everywhere — history is often driven by circumstance.

quiz.q: Why do some historians call the Agricultural Revolution a mixed blessing?
options: Early farmers often worked harder, ate worse, and faced new disease and inequality
It had no effect on society
quiz.explain: For individuals, early farming often meant longer hours, poorer diets, more disease, and the first real inequality — even as it produced more people and power overall.
